newsitem.title: USA: Big Three U.S. May auto sales seen down from '96.
newsitem.headline: Big Three U.S. May auto sales seen down from '96.

text.p: The Big Three automakers are expected to report a down month for U.S. May light vehicle sales, and analysts said labor strikes against General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp. had a minimal effect on the decline.
Unit sales for the total U.S. industry last month are likely to have been flat or down slightly, as the industry made a modest recovery from a surprisingly weak April.
"We anticipate some bounceback, but not to the magnitude of what some people are anticipating," said Paul Ballew, chief economist for industry consultant J.D. Power and Associates.

Analysts' estimates for May's seasonally adjusted annual sales rate range from the middle-14 million units to 15 million units. The April rate was 14.3 million, the lowest seasonally adjusted rate since late 1995. The rate in May 1996 was 15.4 million.
Slow sales continued to plague Detroit's Big Three, according to Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas.
He predicts the group will report sales down 9.6 percent from May 1996, while Japanese automakers continued to chip away at the domestics' market share.

Chrysler will post the weakest results, Colas said, falling a total of 17 percent from a year ago. Passenger car sales continued poor, he said. Chrysler's normally hot-selling light truck segment, which includes minivans, pickup trucks and sport/utilty vehicles, could fall as much as 17 percent, Colas said.

GM is expected to report a nine percent decline in total sales, predicted Burnham Securities Inc analyst David Healy. Light truck sales will be reported as flat, but cars will show a fall of 14 percent, he said.

Ford Motor Co is expected to make the best showing of the Big Three. Analysts said a modest increase in light truck sales should partly offset continued poor car demand, for an estimated total company decline of about five percent.
"I don't think you can blame the strikes at GM and Chrysler for any great degree of those declines," said Healy.
Healy said both GM and Chrysler are up against strong year-ago comparisons. But their slumping sales also reflect the tough competitive environment.

Sales from imports and transplants were down about two percent, Healy said. However, the group's market share continued to creep up, finishing May at an estimated 27.9 percent, compared with 27.6 percent for the first four months of 1997.
Ballew attributed some of the sales softness to capacity shortages among both the Big Three and Japanese automakers.

He said some of the Japanese sales numbers may fall short of estimates because of extremely tight supplies of popular cars such as the Camry and Lexus ES 300 from Toyota Motor Corp and Civic from Honda Motor Co Ltd.
"There are dealers screaming for inventory of those models and the product is just not in the pipeline," he said.
Chrysler is expected to report results June 2, GM on June 3 and Ford on June 4.
